slides.text: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn what to do when your dataset has missing values. First comes the theory: the three reasons data goes missing. Then a hands-on lab in Python, using nearly fifty thousand real New York City Airbnb listings. By the end, you'll be able to detect missing values, work out why they're missing, fill them in four different ways, and judge which fix is best.

No real dataset arrives complete. Forms get skipped, sensors drop out, and some values simply don't exist yet. If you drop every incomplete row, you throw away information. If you fill blindly, you can distort the very statistics you wanted to compute. In our lab data, twenty point six percent of listings are missing the reviews per month value. That's far too many to drop. So the right fix depends on one question: why is the value missing?

Every missing value fits one of three patterns. M C A R, missing completely at random, means the gap has no relationship to any variable. It's pure chance, like a random sensor glitch. M A R, missing at random, means the gap depends on another column you can observe. For example, retired people skip the salary question more often. And M N A R, missing not at random, means the gap depends on the hidden value itself, like high earners declining to report their income. The pattern decides whether an imputation method helps or quietly misleads you.

Let's see this in our data. Reviews per month is missing for 10,116 listings. We checked, and every single one of those rows also has zero reviews. That's the definition of M A R. A listing with no reviews has no reviews per month rate to record, so the gap is fully explained by a column we already have. By contrast, the name and host name columns have only sixteen and twenty-one gaps, scattered with no pattern. That's consistent with M C A R, but be careful: M C A R can never be proven from data alone.

Now the lab. We load the cleaned Airbnb file with pandas. It has 49,195 rows and 16 columns. Calling isnull dot sum gives the missing count for every column. Only four columns have gaps: name, host name, last review, and reviews per month. Everything else is complete.

Counting gaps is easy. Explaining them is the real work. This crosstab compares two things: is reviews per month missing, and is the number of reviews zero. Read the table. When the value is missing, the number of reviews is always zero. And the other two cells are empty. That turns our guess into a verified fact.

One more trap: gaps that isnull cannot see. A price of zero, found in 11 rows, is impossible. A minimum stay of nine hundred ninety-nine nights, in 3 rows, is an old sentinel code. And 8 host names contain the literal text Nan or Na, which pandas reads as a normal string. Convert these to real missing values first. But use judgment. Zero reviews and zero available days are real data, not hidden gaps.

Now to fixing the gaps. Imputation replaces a missing value with an estimate, and every method trades simplicity for how much of the data's real structure it keeps. Mean or median is the quick baseline, but every fill is identical, so it shrinks the variance. K-N-N borrows from similar rows, but it's slower and needs scaled features. Regression predicts the value from other columns, but it can extrapolate poorly.

Method one: mean and median. We compute the fill value from the observed rows only, then fillna applies it to every missing row at once. The observed variance is 2.82. Mean-fill keeps 79.4 percent of it, and median-fill keeps 82.0 percent. Because this column is strongly right-skewed, the median is the more honest single number.

Method two: K-N-N imputation. For each missing row, the imputer finds the five most similar listings by price, location, availability, and the other features, then averages their values. It keeps 86.7 percent of the variance, the best of the four. And for the originally missing rows it filled an average of 0.41, far below the blind mean-fill of 1.37. K-N-N was never told about the zero reviews rule, yet it respected it.

Method three: regression. We train a linear model on the rows where the value is known, then predict the missing ones, clipping at zero because a review rate can't be negative. The R squared is only 0.33, a modest fit. The model predicts 0.78 for the zero-review rows, too high compared with K-N-N. Variance retained is 81.9 percent, about the same as the median. A weak R squared is a warning sign, not a free pass.

Here's what each fill does to the distribution. On the left, the observed data. In the middle, mean-filling stacks more than ten thousand rows on one single value. On the right, K-N-N keeps a natural spread. That's what losing variance looks like.

Lined up side by side, the trade-offs become numbers. Mean retains 79.4 percent, regression 81.9, median 82.0, and K-N-N 86.7. Every method loses some spread, because filling in a guess can never add real information. The lesson isn't never use the mean. It's that checking the variance change is part of the audit.

Let's recap. One: the mechanism, M C A R, M A R, or M N A R, should drive your fix. Two: prove M A R with a crosstab instead of guessing. Three: hunt for disguised gaps before you impute. Four: mean and median are simplest but lose the most variance, while K-N-N kept the most. And five: always compare strategies and check the variance change.

Now try it yourself. Run the detection steps on a column in your own dataset, note which observed column explains the gaps, and compare at least two imputation methods. In the next lesson we'll tackle outliers. If this helped, subscribe so you don't miss it. Thanks for watching.
